headline: Hyperscalers rewarded, Apple punished as Q2 earnings season peaks; GDP slowed to 1.5% and employment costs ran hot, leaving the Fed on hold with real rates at 2.47%.
stance: The market is sending a clear bifurcation signal: cloud and AI infrastructure spending is being rewarded — Amazon and Microsoft surged on massive AWS and Azure beats — while Apple's miss on Services and China revenues drew a sharp ~9% sell-off on Thursday. Q2 GDP came in at 1.5% annualised, the softest quarter since late 2024, and employment costs printed slightly above consensus; neither print changes the Fed's calculus materially. With the S&P 500's Thursday close at 7,489.72 and real rates still at 2.47%, the equity risk premium is negative (-2.15%) and CAPE stands at 40.9 — valuations leave little margin for error if the growth deceleration deepens.

news.head: Amazon Q2 blowout
news.body: Amazon reported Q2 revenue of $200.6 billion (+20% YoY) and AWS grew 37% — its fastest pace in 18 quarters — to $42.2 billion, well above the $40.5 billion consensus; operating income rose 43% to $27.5 billion.

news.head: Apple slumps on Services miss
news.body: Apple topped headline estimates (revenue $109.4 billion, EPS $1.91 vs. $1.89 expected) but the stock fell roughly 9% on Thursday after weaker-than-expected Services and China revenues disappointed investors.

news.head: GDP slows to 1.5%
news.body: Q2 real GDP grew at a 1.5% annualised rate, down from 2.1% in Q1, driven by consumer spending and exports but held back by a decline in government spending.

news.head: Employment costs run slightly hot
news.body: The Employment Cost Index rose 0.9% QoQ in Q2, a tick above the 0.8% consensus, keeping the Fed's inflation-sensitive mandate in focus.

news.head: Middle East tensions persist
news.body: US and Iran exchanged strikes again this week; traders are watching for weekend escalation, with Japan sourcing nearly all its crude from the Middle East adding supply-chain complexity.

news.head: Canada tariff friction
news.body: New US tariffs on Canadian goods — with retaliatory measures signalled by Ottawa — represent a fresh drag on North American supply chains heading into H2.

implications: Cloud infrastructure is the clear Q2 earnings winner: Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet all surged on AI-driven demand, while Apple and Meta were punished by the market for differing reasons — watch for rotation within megacap tech.
Q2 GDP at 1.5% with employment costs above consensus is the soft-landing tightrope: growth is slowing but not collapsing, and inflation pressures have not fully cleared — the Fed remains on hold.
Real rates at 2.47% and a negative equity risk premium (-2.15%) mean equities need continued earnings beats to justify CAPE of 40.9; any guidance disappointment will be met with outsized selling.

Positioning: Speculative positioning in S&P 500 futures reached the 85th percentile of its three-year range this week — a new development — meaning speculators are heavily positioned long, a contrarian warning. Separately, VIX futures specs moved to the 10th percentile (also new this week), indicating almost no bullish volatility bets — a contrarian signal that the market may be under-hedged.

watch.head: July payrolls (8:30am ET)
watch.body: Today's jobs report is the most important near-term data point: with GDP at 1.5% and claims at 197K, a payrolls miss could cement rate-cut expectations while a beat cements the Fed's on-hold stance.

watch.head: ISM Manufacturing (10am ET)
watch.body: The July ISM Manufacturing print follows June's solid 53.3; any softening toward contraction territory would sharpen recession concern given the slowing GDP backdrop.

watch.head: Weekend Middle East developments
watch.body: Stonex flagged that market closures frequently see notable reversals in geopolitical strategy on Iran; energy markets and safe-haven trades are most exposed to a weekend surprise.

watch.head: Amazon stock open
watch.body: Amazon rose roughly +8% in after-hours trading on Thursday after its Q2 beat; how the stock opens and holds through today's session will signal whether institutional buyers step in or take profit.

watch.head: Apple damage assessment
watch.body: Apple's roughly 9% Thursday decline may attract dip-buyers today given the headline beat, but Services and China trajectory questions linger into the September quarter.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: Q2 real GDP printed at 1.5% annualised — the softest reading since late 2024 — driven by consumer spending and exports but weighed down by falling government outlays; Thursday's prior close on the 10-year Treasury yield was 4.75% and the 2-year was 4.28%, leaving the 2s10s curve at +47 basis points.

The Employment Cost Index rose 0.9% QoQ in Q2, modestly above the 0.8% estimate, reinforcing that wage pressure has not fully normalised — a key reason real fed funds remain positive at 0.34% and real 10-year rates stand at 2.47%.

The 10-year breakeven inflation rate closed Thursday at 2.28%, suggesting the bond market sees inflation broadly under control even as employment costs firm — the tension between those two readings is the Fed's current dilemma.

The MOVE index closed at 83 on Thursday — a relatively calm level — while the term premium sits at 83.8 basis points, meaning investors are still demanding meaningful compensation to hold long-dated Treasuries.
Financial conditions remain accommodative: commercial paper spreads are negligible at 25 basis points, IG OAS closed at 80 basis points, and HY spreads were 284 basis points as of Wednesday's close.
sections.positioning: Speculators in 3-month SOFR futures hold almost no bullish bets — at the 3-year low for that contract — a standing contrarian-bullish lean on short rates, though this positioning has been in place for 14 weeks and is background context rather than a new development.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: The S&P 500 closed Thursday at 7,489.72, the Nasdaq 100 at 25,373.85, and the Dow at 52,485.03 — all prior cash closes; VIX closed at 15.99 and VXN at 26.

Breadth improved Thursday: 63.4% of S&P 500 members trade above their 50-day moving average and 67.7% above their 200-day, while Nasdaq breadth is narrower at 47.5% above the 50-day and 66.3% above the 200-day.

The equity risk premium is negative at -2.15% using Thursday's close — meaning equities offer no risk premium over risk-free rates on an earnings-yield basis — and CAPE stands at 40.91, both historically elevated readings.

Amazon rose roughly +8% in after-hours trading Thursday after its Q2 beat; Apple fell roughly 9% in Thursday's regular session after reporting Wednesday evening, and Meta fell 8% Thursday following its own earnings release earlier in the week.
Microsoft surged approximately 15% after its Tuesday earnings beat, with Azure growth of 43% driving the move — the stock's gain alone added meaningful points to cap-weighted indices.
sections.positioning: S&P 500 speculative futures positioning reached the 85th percentile of its three-year range this week — a new development flagged by COT data — representing a extended long that historically precedes mean-reversion episodes. VIX futures specs simultaneously moved to the 10th percentile, also new this week, suggesting the market is materially under-hedged relative to recent history. Russell 2000 specs remain at an extended short (13 consecutive weeks), a contrarian-bullish lean on small caps that has not yet resolved.

sections.title: FX & Commodities
bullets: The US dollar index closed Thursday at 99.8; EUR/USD at 1.1527, USD/JPY at 157.4, and GBP/USD at 1.3487 — all prior cash closes.

Gold closed Thursday at $4,098.60 per ounce and silver at $57.775 per ounce; with real 10-year rates at 2.47%, gold's continued strength at these levels reflects geopolitical risk and central bank demand rather than a rate-driven bid.
WTI crude closed at $86.80 and Brent at $90.12 on Thursday; Middle East tensions between the US and Iran are the primary upside risk to energy prices heading into the weekend.

Copper closed at $6.51 per pound Thursday; the copper-to-gold ratio stands at 1.588, a level that historically correlates with moderate global growth expectations — neither recessionary nor strongly expansionary.
Natural gas closed at $2.792, wheat at 638 cents per bushel, and corn at 463.75 cents per bushel on Thursday; uranium closed at $86.50 per pound.
sections.positioning: WTI crude, Brent, and GBP each registered new crowding extremes in COT data this week — all within the past one to five days — representing fresh positioning signals worth monitoring for reversal. Wheat COT sits at the 98th percentile (two weeks running) and copper at the 96th percentile (15 weeks), both background-level extended longs.

sections.title: Liquidity & Credit
bullets: The Fed's balance sheet grew 1.44% year-over-year as of July 29; bank reserves stood at $2,984.6 billion and the Treasury General Account at $910.8 billion as of July 29.

Overnight reverse repo usage fell to $2.2 billion on Thursday — effectively drained — confirming that excess liquidity has largely exited the RRP facility and is now sitting in bank reserves or deployed into risk assets.
M2 money supply grew 5.53% year-over-year through June, a moderate pace that is broadly consistent with nominal GDP growth and does not signal either a liquidity squeeze or an inflationary surge.
IG OAS closed at 80 basis points and HY spreads at 284 basis points as of Wednesday — both historically tight, consistent with risk-on positioning and low near-term default expectations.

Weekly jobless claims for the week ending July 25 came in at 197K, with the four-week average at 203K — both well below recessionary thresholds and consistent with a still-resilient labour market heading into today's payrolls report.
